Structural intervention distance

Source: R/sid.R
mc_sid.Rd

Counts the ordered pairs of responses for which the estimated graph would send one to the wrong adjustment set (Peters and Buehlmann, 2015). For the pair \((i, j)\) the estimate prescribes adjusting for the parents of \(i\) that it carries; the pair is counted when that set is not a valid adjustment set for the effect of \(i\) on \(j\) in the true graph. The distance is zero when the estimate gives a valid adjustment set for every pair, and it is not symmetric in its two arguments.

Usage

mc_sid(truth, estimated, max_members = 1000L)

# S3 method for class 'mcg_sid'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

truth

the true DAG, as a square 0/1 adjacency matrix where a one in position \((a, b)\) means \(a \to b\). It must be acyclic and have no undirected edge.

estimated

the estimated graph with the same number of nodes and the same convention: a DAG, a CPDAG (undirected edges carry a one in both positions), or an object of class "mcg_cpdag".

max_members

cap on the number of members enumerated for a partially directed estimate.

x

an object of class "mcg_sid".

...

ignored.

Value

For a directed estimate, a single number, the count of offending pairs, with the \(R \times R\) 0/1 matrix of the offending ordered pairs attached as the attribute "pairs" (a one in \((i, j)\) marks the pair \((i, j)\)). For a partially directed one, an object of class "mcg_sid", a list with lower and upper, the smallest and largest distance over the members; values, the distance of each member; n_members; which_lower and which_upper, the positions in the member list (as returned by mc_class_members) attaining each end; and truncated. The print method returns x invisibly.

Why it is not the Hamming distance

The structural Hamming distance counts the edges two graphs disagree about and says nothing about what the disagreement costs. Two estimates at the same Hamming distance from the truth can be worth very different things, one still giving the right adjustment set for every pair and the other for none. This distance asks that question instead.

Which adjustment sets count as valid

Validity is decided by the adjustment criterion of Shpitser, VanderWeele and Robins (2010), in the form given by Perkovic et al. (2018), which is necessary and sufficient, and not by the back-door criterion of Pearl (2009). The back-door criterion is sufficient without being necessary: it refuses any set containing a descendant of \(i\), while a descendant that lies on no causal path from \(i\) to \(j\) does no harm, so using it would count pairs the adjustment in fact recovers. Writing \(\mathrm{cn}(i,j)\) for the nodes other than \(i\) on the directed paths from \(i\) to \(j\) in the true graph, and \(\mathrm{forb}(i,j)\) for their descendants (each node counted among its own) together with \(i\), the parent set \(S\) is valid when it does not meet \(\mathrm{forb}(i,j)\) and when it d-separates \(i\) from \(j\) in the graph with the arcs from \(i\) into \(\mathrm{cn}(i,j)\) removed. With no causal path from \(i\) to \(j\) the second condition asks for separation in the whole graph, which is what recovers a null effect.

One case needs care. When \(j\) itself belongs to the adjustment set the formula collapses to the marginal of \(j\), since conditioning on it and averaging over it returns it unchanged. That is right exactly when the effect is null, and wrong otherwise. Reading it as always wrong would make the distance of a graph to itself nonzero, because a parent of \(i\) always sits in its adjustment set and is never its descendant.

A partially directed estimate gives an interval

A completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG) does not prescribe one adjustment set, so the distance is not one number but the range over the members of the class. The members are enumerated with mc_class_members and the result reports the lower and upper end, the member attaining each, and whether the enumeration had to be capped. When it was capped, the interval covers the enumerated members only.

What the distance measures

The reading in terms of interventions, in which a valid adjustment set recovers the effect of one response on another, holds when the true graph is a causal DAG: a structural model with independent exogenous innovations, no unobserved confounding and no selection bias, whose equations are invariant under intervention. Without those assumptions the distance remains a purely graphical measure of disagreement between the two structures, computed from the parent sets of the estimate. It compares graphs and uses no data.

References

Peters, J. and Buehlmann, P. (2015). Structural intervention distance for evaluating causal graphs. Neural Computation 27(3), 771-799. doi:10.1162/NECO_a_00708

Shpitser, I., VanderWeele, T. and Robins, J. M. (2010). On the validity of covariate adjustment for estimating causal effects. Proceedings of the 26th Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence, 527-536.

Perkovic, E., Textor, J., Kalisch, M. and Maathuis, M. H. (2018). Complete graphical characterization and construction of adjustment sets in Markov equivalence classes of ancestral graphs. Journal of Machine Learning Research 18(220), 1-62.

Pearl, J. (2009). Causality: Models, Reasoning and Inference, 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press.

See also

mc_cpdag_metrics for the Hamming-type measures, mc_class_members for the members of a class.

Other equivalence class: mc_class_coefficients(), mc_class_members()

Examples

# truth 1 -> 2 -> 3; an estimate that reverses the first arc
G <- matrix(0L, 3, 3); G[1, 2] <- G[2, 3] <- 1L
H <- matrix(0L, 3, 3); H[2, 1] <- H[2, 3] <- 1L
mc_sid(G, H)
#> [1] 3
#> attr(,"pairs")
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    0    1    1
#> [2,]    1    0    0
#> [3,]    0    0    0
mc_sid(G, G)          # zero against itself
#> [1] 0
#> attr(,"pairs")
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    0    0    0
#> [2,]    0    0    0
#> [3,]    0    0    0
